say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today’s question sounds easy: how many ways? But counting every possible way, with none missing and none counted twice, is a skill that mathematicians and programmers use every day.
By the end of today you will make the computer list every case for you, and you will know when its answer is right.
Four puzzles. Do not list them all: find a quick way to count, and be ready to say how you counted. Take your time: there is no race.
First one: how many two-digit numbers are there? Careful, it is not 99!

The bubble tea shop has 3 teas and 2 toppings. Before you list them, write your guess: how many different orders? Now the shop adds sizes M and L. Will the number of orders go up by 2, or double, or something else? Write a prediction.
stuck: Stuck listing: write the first tea, then every topping with it. Then the next tea.
Finished early: add sugar levels 0%, 50% and 100%. Predict the number of orders first, on paper.

say: “3 shirts and 2 pairs of shorts. I fix the red shirt and try every pair of shorts: red with black, red with grey. That is 2. Every shirt gets the same 2, so 3 shirts give 3 groups of 2: 3 × 2 = 6. Add 2 caps: each of the 6 outfits splits into 2, so 12.”
“In code, the outer loop picks the shirt and the inner loop picks the shorts. The inner loop goes all the way round for EACH shirt, so the say block runs 3 × 2 = 6 times.”

“5 friends shaking hands. Friend A shakes 4 hands. B has already shaken A’s, so 3 new ones. C: 2 new. D: 1 new. E: none left. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. Or: 5 people times 4 hands is 20, but each handshake has two people in it, so I counted every one twice: 20 ÷ 2 = 10.”

do: Ask: “Which choice did you fix first? How do you know you have them all?”
Ask: “Point to the inner loop. How many times does it run for one turn of the outer loop?”
Ask: “Have you counted any pair twice? Has anyone shaken their own hand?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Fix the first choice, then run through every second choice.”
Hint 2: “Draw a tree, or a table with a row for each first choice.”
Hint 3: “If the order does not matter, has your method counted each pair twice?”

say: “Why does the multiplication rule work for outfits, but 5 × 5 gives the wrong answer for handshakes between 5 friends?”
ask: “Why does the multiplication rule work for outfits, but 5 × 5 gives the wrong answer for handshakes between 5 friends?”

For outfits, every shirt goes with every pair of shorts and a shirt-and-shorts outfit is different from any other, so 3 × 2 counts each outfit once. For handshakes, 5 × 5 = 25 includes each person with themselves (5 cases) and counts A with B and B with A as two, so 25 − 5 = 20 and 20 ÷ 2 = 10. In code, keep only the pairs with a < b.

say: “Today you counted things that would take ages to list: you fixed one choice, multiplied, and halved when you counted twice. Then the computer listed every case to test you. Notice it, test it, explain why.”

p6l5-title.note: Objective: Count every possible case without missing one or counting one twice: list in order, use the multiplication rule for choices made one after another, take care with order and with 0 in digit puzzles, count handshakes and grid routes, and test each count with nested loops in code. Materials: Laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 (scratch.mit.edu) open, the starter project “Every Order” (one loop that says each tea), mini whiteboards, digit cards 0 to 9, squared paper. Online: Children share their screen when they test code. The tutor shares the starter project as an .sb3 file in the chat (children use File, Load from your computer; no account needed), and the three starter blocks are also on the slide. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Digit cards can be cut from paper. Breakout rooms in pairs for the Explore. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5, warm-up 6.5 to 13, explore 13 to 26 (paper only), mini-lesson 26 to 35.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 35.5 to 40.5, worksheet 40.5 to 75 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 75 to 78 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 78 to 83, exit slip 83 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. Before the lesson: share the starter project “Every Order” as an .sb3 file (a sprite with: set tea to 1, repeat 3: say tea for 1 second, change tea by 1). The sprite says the numbers 1, 2, 3, not the tea names: tell children that teas are numbered 1 = milk, 2 = green, 3 = taro and toppings 1 = pearls, 2 = jelly, so "join tea topping" saying 21 means green with pearls.

p6l5-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE show moment only: after both puzzles, everyone holds their paper to the camera at the same moment (or shows it to you only on camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 6 outfits: red-black, red-white, red-grey, blue-black, blue-white, blue-grey. A drawing or an organised list works. Puzzle 2: 10 games. 5 × 4 = 20 counts every game twice (A against B is the same game as B against A), so halve it. Guessing is fine. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l5-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 10.5. Count it, don’t list it. Four quick counting puzzles (two-digit numbers, multiples of 5, lamp posts, numbers with a 7). Pairs say how they counted. No racing and no points. Click once per card to show its answer (cards go left to right, top row first). Four puzzles only, so the warm-up fits. Answers: 90 two-digit numbers (99 − 10 + 1: counting from 10 to 99 includes both ends); 20 multiples of 5; 11 lamp posts (100 ÷ 10 = 10 gaps, plus 1); 19 numbers with a 7 (7, 17, …, 97 is 10; 70 to 79 is 10; 77 is in both lists, so 10 + 10 − 1). Ask after each: "How did you count without listing?" Praise the "+ 1" fix (fence posts: 11 lamp posts) and the "counted twice" fix (77): both come back today.

p6l5-warm2.note: Minutes 10.5 to 13. Whiteboards, then click to show each answer. 1) 24 2) 900 3) 10. Three questions only. For 3: the inner loop says "hi" twice for each of the 5 turns of the outer loop, 5 × 2 = 10. We use this idea a lot today.

p6l5-explore1.note:
Minutes 13 to 26 (this slide 13 to 17.5). The bubble tea shop: 3 teas and 2 toppings. Pairs list every order on paper, then predict how many there are when sizes M and L are added. The nested loop that lists every order is built once, live, in the mini-lesson. Predict first: The bubble tea shop has 3 teas and 2 toppings. Before you list them, write your guess: how many different orders? Now the shop adds sizes M and L. Will the number of orders go up by 2, or double, or something else? Write a prediction. Paper only in this part: the list and the size prediction. Scratch is NOT opened here: the nested loop is built once, live, in the teaching slide Let the computer list them, so nothing is built twice. Hints: Stuck listing: write the first tea, then every topping with it. Then the next tea. If a pair wants more: add sugar levels 0%, 50% and 100%. Predict the number of orders first, on paper. Online: Children share their screen when they test code. The tutor shares the starter project as an .sb3 file in the chat (children use File, Load from your computer; no account needed), and the three starter blocks are also on the slide. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Digit cards can be cut from paper. Breakout rooms in pairs for the Explore.
Python version (for children who know Python, used in the teaching slide):
teas = ["milk", "green", "taro"]
toppings = ["pearls", "jelly"]
count = 0
for tea in teas:
 for top in toppings:
 print(tea, "tea with", top)
 count = count + 1
print(count, "orders") Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if the shop had 3 teas, 3 sizes (S, M, L) and 3 toppings? Predict how many different orders. Then write how you would check with a list or a loop. Answer: 27 orders (3 × 3 × 3). Fix the tea, then the size, then the topping: three loops inside each other, or a tree with three layers.

p6l5-explore2.note: Minutes 17.5 to 26. Gather pairs (or bring them back from breakout rooms). Ask each, take two or three answers, then share one child’s screen to run their code. Answers: 1) 6 orders; with sizes, 12 (each of the 6 orders comes in 2 sizes: 6 × 2). 2) Fix the tea, go through every topping, then move to the next tea: a list in order, like a tree. Watch for children who add (3 + 2 = 5): ask them to point to all 6 orders on their list.

p6l5-teach1.note: Minutes 26 to 28. Teach. Click 1: the tree appears. Then the three steps, then the caps. Think-aloud: “3 shirts and 2 pairs of shorts. I fix the red shirt and try every pair of shorts: red with black, red with grey. That is 2. Every shirt gets the same 2, so 3 shirts give 3 groups of 2: 3 × 2 = 6. Add 2 caps: each of the 6 outfits splits into 2, so 12.” Name it: "When choices are made one after another, we MULTIPLY. This is called the multiplication rule." Ask: "Why not 3 + 2?" (that counts shirts and shorts, not outfits).

p6l5-we1.note: Minutes 28 to 30. Click through the steps. Ask before each: "How many choices does the next dial have?" For step 3: "Dial 1 can be any of 5. Dial 2 cannot repeat it: 4. Dial 3 cannot repeat either: 3." This prepares the digit-card question on page 1. Enumerated check: 125 codes with repeats, 60 without.

p6l5-try1.note: Minutes 30 to 31.5. Whiteboards up together, then click. a) 5 × 4 = 20. b) 3 × 3 = 9: AA, AB, AC, BA, BB, BC, CA, CB, CC. c) 4 × 3 = 12: gold can go to any of 4, then silver to one of the other 3. Ask: "Why is c not 4 × 4?" (one runner cannot win both).

p6l5-teachcode.note:
Minutes 31.5 to 34.5. Teach the code. This is the ONLY place the nested loop is built (about 3 minutes): share your screen, open the starter project Every Order and drag a second repeat inside the first, live. Think-aloud: “In code, the outer loop picks the shirt and the inner loop picks the shorts. The inner loop goes all the way round for EACH shirt, so the say block runs 3 × 2 = 6 times.” Point at "set shorts to 1": "Why must this go INSIDE the outer loop?" (so the shorts start again from 1 for every shirt; if it were outside, shirt 2 would start at shorts 3 and say 23 and 24, which are not real outfits). "join shirt shorts" sticks the two numbers together: shirt 2 and shorts 1 says 21. Ask: "What would it say with repeat 4 inside?" (3 × 4 = 12 things). 
Python version:
count = 0
for shirt in range(1, 4):
 for shorts in range(1, 3):
 print(shirt, shorts)
 count = count + 1
print(count, "outfits")

p6l5-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Adding the choices instead of multiplying them (4 T-shirts and 3 shorts gives 7 outfits). (2) Counting each handshake twice (7 × 6 = 42) or letting a person shake their own hand. (3) Digit cards: putting 0 at the front of a number, or using the same card twice.

p6l5-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 40.5. 5 minutes. Poses: 1 arms up + standing, 2 arms up + squat, 3 arms up + one leg, 4 arms out + standing, 5 arms out + squat, 6 arms out + one leg. Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p6l5-teachcards.note: Minutes 40.5 to 42.5. Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q2, digit cards). Click through. Think-aloud: "Hundreds: any of 3 cards. Tens: one card is used, so 2 left. Ones: 1 left. 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. I list them in order to check: 247, 274, 427, 472, 724, 742." Then the 0 trap: "02 is not a 2-digit number, so the tens has only 2 choices, but the ones can be 0." Ask: "How many 3-digit numbers from 0, 1, 2?" (2 × 2 × 1 = 4: 102, 120, 201, 210).

p6l5-ws1.note: Minutes 42.5 to 55.5. Walk around (or visit breakout rooms). Ask "How do you know you have them all?" before helping. Q3: insist the trace table is filled BEFORE they run the code. Show this preview, do not read it aloud.

p6l5-ws1ans.note: Minutes 55.5 to 58.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q2 (digit cards: how do you know you have them all?), about 35 seconds a question. Q2a: tens 3 choices (not 0), ones 3 choices (the other three cards). Q2b: 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. Q3: a counts the turns of the outer loop, b the inner loop; b goes back to 1 every time a changes. Full key: (a) 12 (4 × 3) (b) 24 (4 × 3 × 2) (the “at least 40 outfits” part is now in Think harder 4) | (a) 9 (3 choices for the tens, as 0 cannot go first, then 3 for the ones: 3 × 3): 30, 35, 38, 50, 53, 58, 80, 83, 85 (b) 18 (3 × 3 × 2) | (a) a 1, b 1: 11; 1, 2: 12; 1, 3: 13; 1, 4: 14; 2, 1: 21; 2, 2: 22 (b) 12 (3 × 4) (c) 34 (d) 20 (5 × 4)

p6l5-ws2.note: Minutes 61.5 to 71.5. Children work alone on Q4 and Q6; Q5 (routes) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Children who finish Q6 build it in Scratch (or Python) and check that it agrees with Q4.

p6l5-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71.5 to 75. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q4 (why 42 ÷ 2). Q5 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home, and you take it up at the start of the next lesson. Q5 corner numbers (bottom row first): 1 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 4 / 1 3 6 10 / 1 4 10 20. With 0 at P: 1 1 1 1 / 1 0 1 2 / 1 1 2 4 / 1 2 4 8. Q6: the "if" is checked 7 × 7 = 49 times. Full key: (a) 21 (6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1) (b) Every handshake has been counted twice, once for each person: 42 ÷ 2 = 21. (the “45 handshakes” part is now in Think harder 4) | (a) 20 (corner numbers, bottom row up: 1 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 4 / 1 3 6 10 / 1 4 10 20) (b) 8 (put 0 at P: 1 1 1 1 / 1 0 1 2 / 1 1 2 4 / 1 2 4 8). 12 routes go through P. | Gaps: repeat 7, repeat 7, if a < b (a > b also works: either keeps each pair once). (a) 21, the same as Q4(a); the “if” is checked 7 × 7 = 49 times. (b) It says 7: it counts each person with themselves (a = b), which is not a handshake.

p6l5-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Extra questions for any pair that wants them (these are not on the Think harder page). Answers: 1) 9 (6 corners make 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15 lines; 6 of them are sides, so 9 are diagonals) 2) 10 (4 of length 1, 3 of length 2, 2 of length 3, 1 of length 4) 3) 120 (5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1); 24 with Ali at the front (4 × 3 × 2 × 1)

p6l5-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are also on the Go further page. Answers: 1) 28 (7 doubles, plus 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21 with two different numbers) 2) 15 (first digit 1: 5 numbers, 2: 4, 3: 3, 4: 2, 5: 1; they are 104, 113, 122, 131, 140, 203, 212, 221, 230, 302, 311, 320, 401, 410, 500)

p6l5-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Which earlier idea does the domino set remind you of? (handshakes) How can a table keep the digit list in order?

p6l5-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: a domino with two different numbers is a pair of numbers from 0 to 6 where order does not matter: exactly the handshake idea with 7 "friends" (21), plus the 7 doubles. Q2: listing by first digit keeps the list in order; the counts 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 are another hidden handshake pattern. A program can test it: for every number from 100 to 999, add up the digits and count the ones that make 5 (it says 15).

p6l5-talk.note: Minutes 78 to 83. One question only. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then volunteers share. Second question (only if flex is left; otherwise the opener of the next lesson): “How would you change a program that lists every pair so that it lists each handshake once?” Answer: For outfits, every shirt goes with every pair of shorts and a shirt-and-shorts outfit is different from any other, so 3 × 2 counts each outfit once. For handshakes, 5 × 5 = 25 includes each person with themselves (5 cases) and counts A with B and B with A as two, so 25 − 5 = 20 and 20 ÷ 2 = 10. In code, keep only the pairs with a < b. Close: “Today you counted things that would take ages to list: you fixed one choice, multiplied, and halved when you counted twice. Then the computer listed every case to test you. Notice it, test it, explain why.”

p6l5-exit.note: Minutes 83 to 86. Answer: 15 (5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1, or 6 × 5 ÷ 2). Extension: Write a program that counts every 3-digit number whose digits add up to 5 (three loops, one inside another). Then change 5 to other totals: which total gives the most numbers?

p6l5-reflect.note: Minutes 86 to 88. Looking back is 2 full minutes, after the exit slip, and is never shortened. Everyone has the box: it is on the Finish page, a page every child reaches. Say: "Two minutes, just for you. Finish: something I did well, the hardest part was, and tick what helped. You can write pass. If you are still stuck, tick that box and I will check in with you in the open session, in the shared room, with your parent nearby." Never collect it in front of the group and never read an answer out. You may look at a child's box on camera in the open session if the child offers it. Praise the strategy, not the speed: say "you you listed them in order, and that is what got you unstuck", never "you were quick". If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session the same day: visit the shared breakout room or use a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never by private message. If a child writes "everything" or "I am bad at maths", say quietly in the open session: "Thank you for telling me. Let's find one small thing that worked today," and point to a specific item they got right. If a child writes that nothing was hard, ask what would make it harder.
